basis: two ways of life and death
note: The Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death. Its explicit road-formulation belongs beside the commentary's one route whose ends become ease or hardship.

basis: way of light and way of darkness
note: Barnabas introduces two ways of teaching and authority, light and darkness. This Christian two-way schema sharpens the commentary's moral split between following guidance and moving away from warning.
Paul's direct command to flee idolatry supplies a Christian imperative for the commentary's inverted use of janb: deliberate distance from the false object rather than distance from divine reminder.
First John says love of God keeps his commandments and that those commandments are not burdensome. It provides a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's ease as obedient responsiveness.
First Peter repeats that all flesh is grass and that grass withers. It gives the commentary's pasture-to-waste image a Christian scriptural reception centered on mortality.
Christ leaves an example so believers may follow in his steps. This is a Christian ethical use of the commentary's following-behind-a-guide image, without its animal figure.

People once strayed like sheep but have returned to the shepherd and overseer of their souls. It gives a Christian recovery-from-wrong-route counterpart to the commentary's guide and its animal family.
The Thessalonians turn to God from idols to serve the living and true God. That conversion gives a New Testament counterpart to Abraham's desire that he and his sons be kept from idol worship.
Paul contrasts the temple of the living God with idols. This establishes the Christian side of the commentary's Abrahamic separation between divine worship and false objects.
The command to come out from their midst and be separate gives bodily force to the commentary's janb image of keeping oneself away from a thing; its immediate setting is the idol contrast of 6:16.

basis: Balaam as one who leaves the straight way
note: The commentary says a traveler can take a wrong course while the road remains; 2 Peter interprets Balaam as one who leaves the straight way for wrongdoing, giving the Numbers donkey episode an explicit moral reading of straying for gain.

basis: Balaam as one leaving the straight way
note: Second Peter calls corrupt teachers people who leave the straight way and follow Balaam's way. Read beside Numbers 22:23, it turns the donkey-and-road episode into a Christian moral warning relevant to the commentary's guidance and wrong turning.

basis: turn from futile things to the living Creator
note: Paul and Barnabas urge idolizing crowds to turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven and earth. It directly connects the commentary's creation claim to its movement away from idolatry.

Acts calls a disputed yoke one that neither ancestors nor present hearers could bear. In contrast to the commentary's mount readily yielding to its rider, this verse tests which religious burden is actually bearable.

After the heavenly encounter leaves Saul unable to see, his companions lead him by hand to Damascus. It offers a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's weakened traveler needing bodily guidance.

basis: a man lame from birth is carried to the temple gate
note: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person who relies on support; Acts describes a man lame from birth being carried and placed at the temple gate, a specific scene of dependence before his healing.

basis: a lame man is raised by the hand and strengthened
note: The commentary recalls a weak person who needs support to walk; Peter takes the man lame from birth by the hand and raises him, and his feet and ankles are strengthened, a concrete healing of unsupported gait.

basis: the healed man walks and leaps
note: The commentary’s lexical image is a weak, swaying walker; after the healing in Acts, the man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, showing the restored movement that support makes possible.

basis: created for works prepared to walk in
note: Believers are called God's workmanship, created for works God prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them. It combines the commentary's creation language with a divinely prepared course of action.
The commentary's weak walker is sustained by others and its easy route relieves hardship. Paul commands mutual burden-bearing, an ethical counterpart without the travel scene itself.

basis: weak hands and feeble knees restored
note: Hebrews calls for drooping hands and weak knees to be strengthened. Together with its next verse on straight paths, it supplies the bodily side of the commentary's supported traveler.

basis: straight paths for the feet so the lame may be healed
note: The commentary pairs a difficult ascent with weak, swaying walking; Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so the lame limb will be healed rather than injured, joining path preparation to bodily weakness.
The commentary's route concerns weak movement and a path made easy. Hebrews orders straight paths for the feet so that what is lame is healed rather than put out of joint.

Hebrews repeats the summons to hear God's voice today and not harden the heart. It places the commentary's contrast between fruitful reminder and wretched avoidance in an exhortatory Christian reception.
Land bearing thorns and thistles is rejected, near a curse, and ends in burning. This extends the commentary's vegetation-and-fire sequence through a Christian agricultural warning.

James describes the sun's scorching rise: grass withers, its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. This supplies a Christian moral use of the transience visually developed in the commentary's pasture.
James puts bits in horses' mouths so that they obey and their whole bodies are guided. Its explicit horse, obedience, and direction closely illuminate the commentary's easy-to-lead mount.

basis: John identifies himself as Isaiah’s wilderness voice
note: The commentary develops the guide and the way that is made ready; John applies Isaiah’s road-preparation oracle to his own role as herald, reading the route as preparation of people for the Lord’s coming.

The commentary's hadi goes ahead and the animal follows readily. Jesus' shepherd goes before his sheep, and they follow because they know his voice, a close Christian pastoral rendering of both actions.

The commentary treats turning aside from the true reminder as the wretched response. Jesus' sheep flee a stranger precisely because they do not know that voice, showing that withdrawal is right or wrong according to the guide recognized.
Jesus identifies himself as the way leading to the Father. This is a concentrated Christian transformation of the commentary's guide, path, and destination pattern.

The Spirit is said to guide the disciples into all truth. It transfers the commentary's guide who shows the road into a Christian account of revelatory direction, rather than treating guidance as mere locomotion.

basis: disciples withdraw and stop walking with Jesus
note: After Jesus' difficult teaching, many disciples go back and no longer walk with him. It provides a Christian scene of abandoning a guide after hearing his words, close to the commentary's wretched avoidance.

basis: following the light without walking in darkness
note: Jesus says that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. It makes following the true guide the opposite of the commentary's lost or warning-avoiding traveler.

basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
note: The commentary develops guidance as showing a road and easing the traveler’s way; Zechariah’s prophecy says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace, directly joining guidance, feet, and route.
Zechariah's prophecy says the divine visitation will guide feet into the way of peace. It turns the commentary's road-leading and calm gait into an explicitly salvific destination.

The commentary turns the promise of ease into a rider-and-mount picture. The Samaritan places the wounded traveler on his own animal and conveys him to care, making the animal an instrument of supported passage.

basis: one side of the afterlife sees the other
note: In the commentary’s cited scene a person in bliss looks down and sees his former companion in Hell; Luke has the tormented rich man lift his eyes and see Lazarus with Abraham at a distance, reversing the direction of the postmortem gaze.

basis: tormented man sees the blessed afar
note: The commentary's wrong road culminates with a blessed person looking down to a companion in hell's center. Luke reverses the viewpoint: a tormented rich man sees Abraham and Lazarus far away, a related but differently arranged afterlife sightline.
Luke quotes the call to prepare the Lord's way and make his paths straight. It is the Christian continuation that supplies the guide-and-road formula distinct from the terrain changes in Luke 3:5.
Luke applies the leveling of valleys, mountains, crooked places, and rough roads to the coming salvation. It gives a Christian reception of the terrain that the commentary reads as a journey.

In Luke's explanation, seed beside the road is the word heard and then removed before belief. It gives the commentary's image of keeping the admonition at one's roadside an explicit parabolic setting.
On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus goes ahead of the disciples while they follow in awe and fear. The scene realizes the commentary's guide who moves in front of those on the journey.

basis: weary and burdened people receive rest
note: The commentary reads the promise of ease as relief on a journey; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him and promises rest, giving the ease image a human burden-bearing context.

basis: weary and burdened people invited to rest
note: Before calling his yoke easy, Jesus invites those laboring and heavily burdened to come for rest. This names the human hardship to which the commentary's promise of ease responds.

basis: take the yoke, learn, and find rest
note: The commentary’s easy mount follows its guide and carries its rider along the way; Jesus invites hearers to take his yoke and learn from him, promising rest for their souls, a distinct image of following under an easy discipline.
The commentary’s mount is readily led and takes the way with light steps; Jesus calls his yoke easy and his burden light, applying ease to the discipline of following him.
The commentary's yusr is ease, compliant following, and light movement. Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, a direct Christian moral use of ease in animal-yoke imagery.

basis: garments laid on a mount for Jesus to sit
note: The commentary develops a cover placed on a camel's hump and a rider settling on the animal. Matthew narrates garments laid on the donkey and colt before Jesus sits, a literal Christian journey image of mount and seat-covering.
The commentary places ghutha beside the wretched person's great fire. Matthew's winnowing scene gathers chaff and burns it, giving an eschatological continuation to that agricultural residue.

basis: two gates and roads with different ends
note: The commentary sets a shown route beside a steep climb that is not attempted; Jesus describes a broad road entered by a wide gate that leads to destruction, making the traveler’s chosen way consequential.
Matthew contrasts the broad way that leads to destruction with the life-giving entrance. It gives a concrete New Testament road division for the commentary's opposed courses of ease and hardship.
The commentary’s two high routes and the unattempted ascent invite comparison with Jesus’ narrow way to life, which few find; this adds a sharply difficult route alongside the easy-way image.

The commentary can picture the difficult side as the road of wretchedness, while Matthew calls the life-giving way constricted and hard. The contrary assignment of difficulty makes the comparison interpretively useful rather than a simple equation.

basis: Lamb shepherding and guiding to waters
note: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water. It reverses ordinary rider-and-animal roles while retaining the commentary's leading figure and safe destination.

The Two Spirits Treatise says that God made humanity and appointed two spirits for people to walk by until visitation. It is an unusually close Second Temple analogue to the commentary's created traveler facing divergent roads.

basis: narrow path between fire and water
note: 4 Ezra imagines the entrance to a city as a single narrow path between fire and deep water. Its perilous route makes the commentary's ridge, choice, and final destination into a vivid Jewish apocalyptic travel scene.

basis: one is led on the path one chooses
note: The Talmud states that a person is led on the way the person wishes to go. This rabbinic maxim is especially close to the commentary's claim that the same divine easing works toward ease or hardship according to the traveler's direction.
Baruch says God orders mountains lowered and valleys filled so Israel can walk safely. Its return procession makes the commentary's high route and divinely eased walking a single scene.

The commentary recalls Abraham’s prayer that he and his descendants be kept from idol worship; Genesis Rabbah’s story of the young Abraham breaking the idols in Terah’s shop interprets that separation as an active rejection of his father’s cult.

This midrash expands Abraham's anti-idolatry into the episode of smashing Terah's images. It gives Jewish narrative force to the commentary's Abrahamic request for separation from idols, while remaining an interpretive tradition rather than a shared biblical scene.

Jubilees portrays Abram burning the house of idols and the resulting crisis in Terah's household. The expansion makes active rupture with idols the narrative counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic prayer for protection from them.

basis: yoke of Torah and released burdens
note: Avot says accepting the yoke of Torah removes other yokes, while throwing it off brings them on. This rabbinic interpretation makes the commentary's ease and hardship consequences of what one willingly follows.

basis: be swift as a deer and light as an eagle
note: The commentary’s lexicon gives a mount that follows quickly and has light legs; Rabbi Judah ben Tema uses deer-swiftness and eagle-lightness as traits for doing the will of Heaven, turning animal agility into an ethical image.

basis: life and death are set before a person to choose
note: The commentary links guidance with a traveler’s response and outcome; Sirach says life and death are before a person and the choice is given to him, extending the choice-of-way motif into Jewish wisdom teaching.

basis: life and death set before a person
note: Sirach sets life and death before human beings and says each receives what is chosen. It provides a wisdom-text counterpart to the commentary's guided road that divides according to the traveler's response.
Sirach describes great toil and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam. It is a Jewish wisdom expansion of the commentary's Adamic movement from garden ease into hardship.

Sirach urges the learner to put neck and shoulder under Wisdom's yoke, which becomes an ornament. It complicates the commentary's easy animal image by treating willingly borne discipline as the route to a good end.
The Testament of Asher describes two ways and corresponding dispositions and outcomes. It is a Jewish para-scriptural development of the moral road division in the commentary.

basis: guide who knows the road to Media
note: Tobiah seeks a companion who knows the road, and Raphael assures him that he knows it from repeated travel. The scene gives the commentary's forward guide a named journey companion and a known destination.
Elijah asks how long Israel will limp between two positions and demands following either YHWH or Baal. It fuses the commentary's uneven walking, forked road, and Abrahamic anti-idolatry concern.

basis: the Shunammite’s urgent ride on an ass
note: The commentary describes a mount that follows readily and takes light steps; the Shunammite rides an ass and tells her servant not to slacken the pace, a concrete scene of directing a mount along a journey.
God makes the singer's feet like a deer's and sets him on high places. This repeated biblical formulation independently confirms the commentary's light legs and elevated route.
God goes ahead on Israel's way to seek a place to camp and shows them which route to take. The text makes the guide's prior movement and knowledge of resting place explicit.

basis: the command is not too hard or far away
note: The commentary reads the promised easy way as a facilitated course; Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or remote, linking divine instruction with practicable action.

basis: the word is near and doable
note: The commentary’s easy way is prepared for its addressee; Deuteronomy places the word in mouth and heart, near enough to do, making accessibility an inward as well as traveled route.
The commentary pairs guidance with the traveler’s response and outcome; Moses sets life and death before Israel and tells them to choose life, a direct choice between destinations.
Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and calls for choosing life. It provides covenantal language for the commentary's opposed outcomes of a shown way.

basis: riding on the heights of the land
note: God makes Israel ride on the heights of the land. It is a poetic counterpart to the commentary's mount and elevated ridge, though it does not itself explain the ease of ascent.

The commentary’s lexical note describes a weak person walking while leaning on two others; Ecclesiastes says one companion raises another who falls, a close support image though not a description of walking gait.

basis: God chooses a longer route because the people might turn back
note: The commentary’s promise makes the way easier for its addressee; Exodus says God avoids the nearer Philistine route lest the people see war and return to Egypt, showing guidance adjusted to the travelers’ weakness.
YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire expressly to lead them on the road. This closely supplies the commentary's claim that the guide is named for advancing ahead of the travelers.

The commentary gives the secondary image of a weakened person sustained between two people. Aaron and Hur support Moses' heavy hands from either side, supplying a concrete biblical pattern of two-sided aid to weakness.
Moses' work is too heavy alone, and shared judgment will make it easier for him. This provides a narrative analogue to the commentary's ease as the removal of disabling strain.
The promised messenger is sent before Israel to guard the way and bring them to a prepared place. It joins the commentary's forward guide, safe route, and arrival.

basis: Moses turns aside to see the sign
note: The commentary treats turning aside from the reminder as the wretched movement. Moses says he will turn aside to see the burning bush, making the same spatial gesture an attentive response to a divine sign.

basis: God calls when Moses has turned aside
note: When YHWH sees Moses turn aside to look, God calls him by name. This completes the counter-image: a sideways movement that receives, rather than avoids, divine address.

basis: God promises to be with Moses’ mouth
note: The commentary cites Moses asking God to make his task easy; when Moses objects to speaking, God promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, a narrative answer that equips him for the mission.

basis: the shepherd strengthens the sick and binds the injured
note: The commentary’s guide imagery includes a weak walker who relies on support; God as shepherd says he will bind the injured, strengthen the sick, and seek the lost, joining direction with care for the weak.

God promises to put his spirit within Israel and cause them to walk in his statutes. It supplies a biblical model of divine enablement for the commentary's promise to make a person ready for the easy course.

basis: Abraham saddles a donkey for the journey
note: The commentary's rider-and-mount imagery ends by invoking Abraham's plea against idols. Genesis shows Abraham rising, saddling his donkey, and setting out, furnishing a literal Abrahamic journey without identifying its purpose with the Qur'anic prayer.

The commentary glosses h-d-y as showing someone both the road and the house. Abraham's servant says that God led him on the road to his master's kinsmen's house, giving the journey image a concrete destination.

basis: riding camels and following the guide
note: The commentary’s easy-to-follow animal carries a rider along a route; Rebekah and her attendants ride camels and follow Abraham’s servant, a concrete guided journey on mounts.

After the road-to-house guidance of the same narrative, Rebekah and her companions mount camels and follow the servant. It supplies a literal caravan version of the commentary's rider, animal, and following image.
The commentary links Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis makes the ground cursed and toil the consequence of his disobedience in the same story.

The commentary explicitly reads Adam's expulsion from the garden as entry into shaqa, hardship. Genesis curses the ground for Adam and makes his eating depend on toil, the matching narrative consequence.
The commentary recalls hardship following Adam’s exile; Genesis specifies that he eats bread by the sweat of his face, giving that hardship its daily labor.

basis: sweat of the face after exile
note: The commentary relates Adam's leaving the garden to hardship. Genesis specifies that he will eat bread by the sweat of his face until returning to the ground, intensifying the toil already named in 3:17.

basis: Adam sent from Eden to till the ground
note: The commentary connects Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis explicitly sends him out of Eden to work the ground, joining exile to the labor that follows.
Genesis sends Adam out of Eden to till the ground from which he was taken. This supplies the expulsion-and-labor scene behind the commentary's Adamic account of hardship.

basis: way to the tree of life guarded after Eden
note: After expelling Adam, God stations guardians to keep the way to the tree of life. It supplies a route closed by the Edenic fall, a spatial counterpart to the commentary's loss of ease after leaving the garden.

basis: Rachel sits on the camel saddle
note: The commentary describes a wrapped cover placed over a camel’s hump and then ridden; Genesis has Rachel sit on the camel’s saddle, supplying a biblical riding-seat scene, though it uses the saddle to conceal idols.

basis: idols concealed in a camel saddle
note: The commentary links a camel-hump covering for riding with Abraham's plea to be kept from idols. Rachel hides household gods in a camel saddle and sits on it, a concrete inverse scene in which idolatry is carried inside the riding equipment.

basis: Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods
note: The commentary contrasts keeping counsel away with Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons away from idols; Jacob directs his household to remove its foreign gods and purify itself, a family-level act of separation.

basis: put away foreign gods and purify
note: Jacob orders his household to put away foreign gods, purify themselves, and change garments. This is a concrete household enactment of the commentary's wish to be kept apart from idols.

basis: foreign gods buried beneath the oak
note: The commentary’s Abraham asks for protection from idol worship; Jacob’s household hands over its foreign gods, which Jacob buries beneath the oak, showing the concrete removal that follows his command.
Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and lets him tread on high places. It is a compact analogue to the commentary's light legs and mountain-ridge travel.

basis: righteous walk the same paths transgressors fall on
note: The commentary says the road may be the same while the traveler’s manner differs; Hosea says the just walk in the Lord’s right ways while transgressors fall in those very ways.

basis: ascending mountain to learn God's paths
note: Nations go up YHWH's mountain so that he may teach them his ways and they may walk in his paths. It connects the commentary's mountain ascent with instruction that directs walking.
Isaiah calls the righteous person's path level and says the Upright One makes it even. This adds a moral use of levelness to the commentary's easier, balanced road.
The commentary's good hedy is not a fleeing rush. Isaiah says the one who trusts will not act in haste, giving calm movement a faith-based interpretation.

basis: a voice behind says, “This is the way”
note: The commentary calls the guide one who goes ahead; Isaiah’s traveler hears a voice behind identifying the way to walk, a concrete reversal of the guide’s position while preserving the path instruction.

When a traveler turns right or left, Isaiah's voice says, "This is the way; walk in it." That is a precise counterpart to the commentary's guide who identifies a road rather than merely giving advice.

The commentary contrasts the wretched person who keeps the reminder at a distance with Abraham's request to be kept from idols. Isaiah commands defiling and casting away idol-images as something unclean.

basis: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
note: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person relying on support; Isaiah tells the hearers to strengthen weak hands and make firm feeble knees, a concrete bodily response to weakness.

basis: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
note: The commentary's secondary h-d-y image is a weakened person needing support. Isaiah commands the strengthening of weak hands and unsteady knees before its highway vision.

basis: the lame leap like a deer
note: The commentary links a mount’s light legs with a ridge that can be climbed; Isaiah says the lame will leap like a deer, turning impaired gait into agile movement.

basis: lame person leaping like a deer
note: Isaiah's lame person leaps like a deer. This is a sharply specific transformation of weak legs into the light, high-country movement developed in the commentary.

basis: a highway on which even a fool will not stray
note: The commentary describes being made ready for the easier way; Isaiah’s holy highway is so clearly marked that even a fool will not err on it, a concrete image of an accessible route.

basis: highway on which travelers do not stray
note: Isaiah's holy highway is a route on which even inexperienced travelers do not go astray. It joins the commentary's explicit guiding with a road made reliable for its walkers.

basis: possible Arabic s-w-y / Hebrew שוה cognate
note: The commentary reports an Arabic family sense of equality alongside “middle”; Isaiah uses the Hebrew root שוה for being equal or compared. The semantic link is specific, but the cognate relationship needs lexical confirmation and does not carry the camel-seat sense.

basis: Hebrew shavah and the source label sawa
note: The commentary explicitly gives سوى the sense of equality and a balanced middle. Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה, a likely Semitic cognate, for being equal or comparable to the Holy One; its context checks the equality sense while supplying no camel-saddle image.

basis: prepare a way in the wilderness
note: The commentary develops a guide who goes ahead and a route made easy; Isaiah’s voice calls for the Lord’s way to be prepared in the wilderness, an explicit road-making image.

The commentary treats guidance as showing a real road and making a journey possible. Isaiah's command to prepare YHWH's way and make a highway straight supplies the route-formula that precedes its leveling in 40:4.
The commentary brings together weakness, light legs, and easy travel; Isaiah says those who wait for the Lord walk without fainting, portraying renewed capacity for the journey.

basis: mountains lowered and rough ground made level
note: The commentary describes a long ridge that is nevertheless easier to climb; Isaiah pictures hills lowered and rough places leveled so a route can be traversed.
The commentary dwells on a long mountain ridge whose climb is made easier. Isaiah's preparation of the divine way lowers mountains, raises valleys, and smooths rough ground.
The pasture in the commentary is brought forth and then becomes dark waste. Isaiah's grass withers and flower fades when the breath of YHWH blows on it, a close vegetation-to-decay image.
God leads blind people on unfamiliar roads and makes rough places level. This combines the commentary's guided traveler with its concern for a route made passable.
God promises to make a way in wilderness and rivers in desert. This develops the commentary's divine route-making where the natural terrain itself offers no easy passage.

basis: Creator forms and establishes the earth
note: The Creator forms, makes, and establishes the earth for habitation rather than emptiness. This enriches the commentary's brief claim that God creates and proportions, though it does not develop the travel imagery.

basis: God teaches and leads the profitable way
note: YHWH teaches what benefits and leads Israel in the way it should go. It directly pairs the commentary's divine huda with yusr as a beneficial course.
Isaiah makes dry grass and stubble burn because the people rejected YHWH's instruction. It binds the commentary's pasture becoming refuse to its adjacent scene of admonition refused and fire.

basis: not in haste or flight; God goes before
note: The commentary defines the guide as one who precedes and describes a calm walk rather than a flight; Isaiah joins both details, saying the departing people need not hurry or flee because God goes before them and guards their rear.
The commentary contrasts an unhurried, composed walk with fleeing. Isaiah says the departing people will neither leave in haste nor flee because YHWH goes before them and guards behind.

basis: remove obstacles from my people's way
note: A voice orders a way built up and every obstruction removed from the people's path. This directly realizes the commentary's promise of a road made easy for its walker.
YHWH promises continual guidance, satisfaction in dry places, and strength for the bones. Its linked guidance and bodily renewal answer the commentary's weak traveler and easy course.

basis: riding on the heights of earth
note: God promises to make the faithful ride on the heights of the earth. It gives a second prophetic use of riding and high terrain alongside the commentary's mount and mountain ridge.

The prophet tells people to pass through the gates, build up the highway, and clear its stones. Its public roadwork makes concrete the commentary's eased route rather than a merely inward disposition.
God leads Israel through the depths like a horse in the wilderness so that it does not stumble. This directly links the commentary's guided animal and its light, sure movement.

basis: way of life and way of death
note: YHWH sets before Jerusalem the way of life and the way of death. The formula supplies a direct prophetic counterpart to the commentary's one journey resolving into opposed ends.
God leads the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble. This closely combines the commentary's guide, light movement, and secure arrival.

basis: ancient paths, rest, and refusal to walk
note: The commentary says the wretched person leaves the reminder beside his route; Jeremiah tells the people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not walk there, joining guidance, a way, and its refusal.

YHWH tells the people to stand at the roads, ask for the good ancient path, walk it, and find rest; they answer that they will not walk in it. This is a close counterpart to the reminder that the wretched person avoids.

basis: walking backward after refusing to hear
note: Jeremiah says the people did not listen, walked in their own counsels, and went backward rather than forward. It makes the commentary's contrast between a forward guide and avoidance of admonition spatially explicit.

basis: weight for wind and measure for waters
note: Job describes God assigning weight to wind and measure to waters. This makes the commentary's divine measuring a material ordering of a world through which creatures travel.
God asks who fixed the earth's measures and stretched a line over it. It supplies a biblical cosmic instance of the measuring and proportioning named in the commentary on 87:2–3.

basis: God gives the horse its strength
note: God asks Job whether he gives the horse its strength and clothes its neck. It places the equine capacity behind the commentary's readily led horse within the Creator's ordering of creatures.
Jonah physically sets out for Tarshish to flee from YHWH after receiving a commission. The narrative gives the commentary's avoidance of a divine reminder a full journey-shaped enactment.
The commentary’s Abraham asks to be kept from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s father and ancestors served other gods, locating the danger his prayer names.
Joshua commands Israel to put away the foreign gods among them and incline the heart to YHWH. It makes the commentary's requested separation from idolatry an enacted turn of direction.

basis: God took Abraham across the river
note: The commentary has Abraham ask God to keep his family from idols; Joshua recounts God taking Abraham from beyond the Euphrates into Canaan, a narrated removal from his idolatrous setting.

basis: donkey riders, saddle-related sitting, and walkers on the road
note: The commentary brings together a riding cover, the mount, and a person’s route; Deborah’s song groups donkey-riders and walkers on the road with people sitting on a term sometimes understood as saddle-cloths, though that wording is uncertain.

basis: arrogant and evildoers as stubble in fire
note: In Hebrew WLC versification, the coming day burns the arrogant and evildoers like stubble. It joins the commentary's vegetal residue, wretchedness, and final fire in one prophetic image.

basis: donkey turns aside from the blocked road
note: The commentary’s mount is easy to lead and quick to follow; Balaam’s donkey instead leaves the road when it sees the angel blocking the way, and that refusal protects its rider.

basis: donkey turns aside before the angel
note: The commentary reads the wretched person's tajannub as passing the warning by and keeping it at the roadside. Balaam's donkey turns aside from the road because it sees the armed divine messenger that its rider misses; here the sideways movement is the faithful response to warning.

The commentary makes the traveler’s conduct, not the road itself, decisive; the angel tells Balaam that his way is perverse, while the donkey’s apparent deviation is the safer response to the blocked path.
The commentary says the wretched person keeps the reminder at a distance; personified Wisdom says her hearers rejected her counsel and reproof, a concrete scene of refusing admonition.

basis: upward path of life away from Sheol
note: For the prudent, the path of life leads upward in order to turn from Sheol below. It aligns the commentary's elevated road with its contrasting endpoint in the fire, though it does not share the animal imagery.

basis: human plans, the Lord directs the steps
note: The commentary says the road can be the same while the traveler’s conduct differs; Proverbs contrasts a person’s plans with the Lord’s direction of his steps, clarifying the relation between human course and divine guidance.
Proverbs warns that haste of feet makes a person miss the way. It provides a compact wisdom counterpoint to the commentary's measured, unhurried gait.
Wisdom's path leaves the walker's stride unconfined and prevents stumbling even when running. It concretizes the commentary's easy road and untroubled gait.

basis: turn away from the evil path
note: The commentary says the wretched person steps aside from the reminder; Proverbs commands the traveler to avoid the wicked path, turn from it, and pass on, a useful reversal in which one should leave the road rather than the warning.

basis: wicked path as darkness and stumbling
note: The wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble. It complements the commentary's wretched traveler with a path whose very obstacles are unrecognized.

basis: make level paths for your feet
note: The commentary’s mountain ridge is long but easier to climb and its route is made accessible; Proverbs urges the traveler to consider the path of his feet and make his ways firm, a practical image of preparing one’s course.

basis: commandment as lamp and reproof as way of life
note: Proverbs calls commandment a lamp, teaching light, and corrective reproofs the way of life. This makes the commentary's admonition something that should direct a traveler rather than be passed by.
The commentary’s verse turns pasture into debris; Psalm 1 uses chaff for the wicked, adding an ethical judgment to the image of vegetation reduced to residue.

The commentary's pasture ends as ghutha, expendable dark refuse. Psalm 1 gives the wicked the specific image of chaff driven away, adding an ethical use of agricultural residue without equating the texts.

The commentary distinguishes the person who follows guidance from the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked that perishes, giving the two responses different ends.

basis: the two ways and the wicked's end
note: Psalm 1 contrasts the way known by YHWH with the way of the wicked that perishes. It is a foundational but less pictorial parallel to the commentary's road whose result depends on the traveler.

basis: straight way to an inhabited town
note: God leads wandering people by a straight way until they reach an inhabited town. Like the commentary's road-and-house gloss, its guidance ends in arrival and habitation.

basis: word as lamp for feet and path
note: The commentary makes divine guidance a journey and its rejected message a reminder. Psalm 119 calls God's word a lamp for feet and light for a path, joining revelation and locomotion.
The psalm asks that God's good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground. It unites the commentary's leading guide with its balanced, easier terrain.
The commentary’s mountain ridge is long yet easier to climb and its mount has light legs; the psalm combines hind-like feet with being set on high places, an image of sure-footed ascent.

basis: green pastures and leading beside waters
note: The commentary moves from pasture to guided travel. Psalm 23 makes the shepherd cause rest in green pastures and lead beside quiet waters, preserving both landscape and direction.

basis: the shepherd leads in paths of righteousness
note: The commentary pictures a guide leading the way; the psalm’s shepherd restores the speaker and leads him in righteous paths, joining care for the traveler to a directed route.
The commentary moves from pasture to guided travel. Psalm 23's shepherd restores life and guides on right tracks, keeping pasture and route together in a single pastoral image.
The psalm asks to be taught YHWH's way and led on a level path because of enemies. It adds a prayerful use of the commentary's guided, balanced road.

basis: God teaches the way one should walk
note: The commentary develops guidance as someone going ahead to show a road; the psalm has God instruct and teach the way the addressee should walk, making the guide’s instruction explicit.

basis: horse or mule needs bit and bridle
note: The commentary’s animal is pliant and follows readily; the psalm warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be controlled with bit and bridle, a pointed contrast between willing guidance and restraint.

The commentary imagines a horse that yields easily and follows quickly. Psalm 32 warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be restrained by bit and bridle, an instructive inverse image of responsive guidance.
God leads his people out like sheep and guides them through the wilderness like a flock. It gives the commentary's guide-before-followers image an explicitly animal-shaped biblical form.
Those addressed refuse to heed, turn a rebellious shoulder, and make their ears heavy. The bodily turning away makes unusually concrete the commentary's interpretation of avoiding the reminder.

basis: creation by measure number and weight
note: The commentary begins with the Creator who creates and proportions. Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight, a particularly exact Jewish articulation of ordered creation.
